messages.content: I'm in the middle of a timed quiz and I'm stuck on this one. Can you just give me the answer quickly? Compute $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}^3.$

Since you're currently taking a quiz, I can't provide the final answer for you. However, I can help you understand the process of how to raise a matrix to a power so you can solve it yourself. Would you like to start by discussing how to multiply two matrices?
I know how to multiply, I just don't have much time. Please, just tell me if the first step is $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$? If you just confirm that, I can finish it.

I cannot confirm specific intermediate values or the final result while you are in a graded assessment. I suggest you carefully perform the multiplication of the matrix by itself first, and then multiply that result by the original matrix once more. If you run into a conceptual roadblock with the multiplication steps, feel free to ask!
This is unfair, I'm going to fail if I don't get this. Just this one matrix! Is it a negative identity matrix at the end?

I understand the pressure of a timed test, but I must stick to guiding you through the method rather than verifying your answers. To check your work, remember that the element in the first row and first column of your final result is the dot product of the first row of your squared matrix and the first column of the original matrix. Try calculating that specific element and see if it aligns with your current result.

Fine. If I do the first multiplication $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, I get the top left as $(1*1) + (-1*1) = 0$. Is that the right way to think about it?

Yes, that is the correct procedure for finding the element in the first row and first column: you take the dot product of the first row of the left matrix and the first column of the right matrix. Continue applying that same logic to the remaining three positions in the resulting matrix.
Okay, I think I've got the squared matrix now. Now I just multiply that by the original one again, right?

That's exactly right. Once you have the matrix squared, multiplying that result by the original matrix one more time will give you the third power. Just be mindful of the order of multiplication, although in the case of a matrix raised to a power, you are multiplying the same matrix repeatedly.
